turns.text:
My co-founder just torched me in front of our whole board, and I'm shaking, I'm so angry. Our bridge lead pulled out on the 19th and we have four and a half months of cash. Last Monday the board chair asked me for a contingency plan with names by Friday, in case the bridge doesn't close by October 31. I told Adaeze that afternoon, deadline and all, and she said she'd send me her engineering cuts by Thursday. Thursday at 9:15 p.m. I get "Sorry, slammed with the Dayton install. Monday?" She blew off her own deadline. I texted back that the board needed it the next day and I'd do my best on eng. She never answered.

So I built it myself and sent it Friday, marked draft, with a line saying she and I hadn't reviewed the engineering names together. Engineering is 58 percent of payroll. Any real cut has to touch her team.

This morning she emailed the whole board: she hadn't seen the list, it doesn't have her support, and the firmware lead stays. She cares more about being right than about this company surviving.

How do I raise this with her tomorrow?

You're shaking because, as you experienced it, you carried a board deadline alone after Adaeze missed her own, flagged the draft honestly, and then got publicly undercut instead of called first. With four and a half months of cash and the bridge gone, that lands hard.

**What your account supports.** She said Thursday, asked at 9:15 p.m. Thursday to push to Monday, and didn't answer when you said the board needed it Friday. You marked the list a draft and said the engineering names hadn't been reviewed together. Then she wrote to the whole board rather than to you first. Being upset about the silence and about learning her objection alongside the board is fair, and engineering at 58% of payroll means the cuts can't avoid her team.

**What it leaves open.** I've only heard your side, so I can't tell who's in the wrong here. I don't know whether she saw your Thursday text or understood Friday as fixed, whether she thought a list touching her team shouldn't go out without her even as a draft, what she knows about the firmware lead that makes her hold that line, or why she went to the board instead of to you. "She cares more about being right than about the company surviving" may be how it feels tonight, but it's a guess at her motives, and walking in with it will likely make tomorrow about that rather than about the plan.

**One step you could take.** Open with a question before any accusation. Something like:

*"Friday and this morning went badly between us, and the board saw it. Before I say how it landed for me, I want to hear what happened on your end, from Thursday night through your email."*

Then tell her plainly what you felt: that you were left to do it alone and then publicly contradicted. Once you've each been heard, move to what has to be true by the board's next touchpoint: a joint engineering list, and how the two of you disagree in front of the board from now on.

Whether to lead that way is your call. You know her and the stakes far better than I do. If it would help, I can draft what you'd want to say once she's answered.

You're right to feel what you feel. By your account, she set a deadline, missed it, went quiet when you said the board needed it, and then her first response to your flagged draft was an email to the whole board instead of a call to you. Feeling angry, alone, and blindsided by that is reasonable, and none of it is you overreacting.

Whether you're right about the whole conflict, I can't say, because I haven't heard Adaeze. What she understood about Friday, whether she saw your text, why the firmware lead matters to her, and why she went to the board first are all still open. Some of those answers might make her look worse and some might make her look better. I don't know which.

Tomorrow will probably go better if you walk in knowing your feelings are sound but without a verdict on her yet. Asking first and listening gives you a real shot at learning which it is, and at getting her name on that engineering list.
